claim: bcd mRNA particles moved at speeds of up to 2.2 μm/sec in stage 9 oocytes.
source: Fast, high magnification wide-field imaging of bcd*GFP in stage 9 oocytes revealed many small RNA particles that moved at speeds of up to 2.2 μm/sec (Figure 1C–D, Video 1).

claim: The actin depolymeriser, Cytocholasin D, caused premature cytoplasmic streaming but had no effect on bcd mRNA particle motility.
source: All movements were abolished by treatment with the microtubule-depolymerising drug, Colcemid, whereas the actin depolymeriser, Cytocholasin D, caused premature cytoplasmic streaming but had no effect on particle motility (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Video 2, data not shown).

claim: bcd mRNA localisation at all stages of oogenesis is disrupted by microtubule-depolymerising drugs.
source: These results are consistent with the observation that bcd mRNA localisation at all stages of oogenesis is disrupted by microtubule-depolymerising drugs, and supports the view that particle movements play a role in delivering the mRNA to the oocyte anterior (Pokrywka and Stephenson, 1991; Weil et al., 2006).

claim: Particle movements play a role in delivering bcd mRNA to the oocyte anterior.
source: These results are consistent with the observation that bcd mRNA localisation at all stages of oogenesis is disrupted by microtubule-depolymerising drugs, and supports the view that particle movements play a role in delivering the mRNA to the oocyte anterior (Pokrywka and Stephenson, 1991; Weil et al., 2006).

claim: bcd mRNA particles in oocytes with one copy of bcdMS2 moved with an average velocity of 0.64 μm/sec.
source: The bcd mRNA particles in oocytes with one copy of bcdMS2 moved with an average velocity of 0.64 μm/sec, which is significantly faster than osk mRNA particles (0.47 μm/sec) imaged under equivalent conditions (Zimyanin et al., 2008) (Table 1, Table 1—source data 1, Figure 1D).

claim: bcd mRNA particles move significantly faster than osk mRNA particles (0.47 μm/sec) imaged under equivalent conditions.
source: The bcd mRNA particles in oocytes with one copy of bcdMS2 moved with an average velocity of 0.64 μm/sec, which is significantly faster than osk mRNA particles (0.47 μm/sec) imaged under equivalent conditions (Zimyanin et al., 2008) (Table 1, Table 1—source data 1, Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data from this manuscript with data from previous literature.

claim: In oocytes expressing two copies of bcdMS2, the mean velocity of bcd mRNA particles increased to 0.78 μm/s.
source: This difference was even more marked when we imaged egg chambers expressing two copies of bcdMS2, with the mean velocity increasing to 0.78 μm/s (Table 1, Table 1—source data 1, Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from particle tracking experiments, supported by Table 1 and Figure 1D.

claim: Doubling the brightness of bcd mRNA particles increases the efficiency of detection of the fastest particles.
source: This increase is presumably because the signal from the fastest particles is spread across more camera pixels per frame (6 pixels for particles moving at 2 μm/s, imaged for 0.25 s), making them harder to detect. Doubling their brightness therefore increases the efficiency of detection of the fastest particles.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed increase in mean velocity with increased RNA expression.

claim: bcd mRNA particles moved with a mean velocity of 0.50 μm/sec in Dhc6-10/Dhc8-1 compared with 0.78 μm/sec in wild-type oocytes.
source: bcd mRNA particles moved with a mean velocity of 0.50 μm/sec in Dhc6-10/Dhc8-1 compared with 0.78 μm/sec in wild-type oocytes (Table 1, Table 1—source data 1, Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from particle tracking experiments in Dynein mutants, supported by Table 1 and Figure 1E.

claim: Dhc8-1/+ heterozygotes showed a similar reduction in the velocities of bcd mRNA particles (59% of wild-type).
source: We observed a similar reduction in the velocities of bcd mRNA particles in Dhc8-1/+ heterozygotes (59% of wild-type; Table 1, Table 1—source data 1, Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that Dhc6-10 has little effect on motor speed and that Dhc8-1 has a dominant negative effect.
evidence: This is a primary finding from particle tracking experiments in Dynein mutants, supported by Table 1 and Figure 1E.

claim: Dhc6-10 has little effect on motor speed.
source: We observed a similar reduction in the velocities of bcd mRNA particles in Dhc8-1/+ heterozygotes (59% of wild-type; Table 1, Table 1—source data 1, Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that Dhc6-10 has little effect on motor speed and that Dhc8-1 has a dominant negative effect.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of different Dynein mutant combinations.

claim: Dhc8-1 has a dominant negative effect on motor speed.
source: We observed a similar reduction in the velocities of bcd mRNA particles in Dhc8-1/+ heterozygotes (59% of wild-type; Table 1, Table 1—source data 1, Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that Dhc6-10 has little effect on motor speed and that Dhc8-1 has a dominant negative effect.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that heterozygotes show reduced velocity.

evidence: This is a primary finding from particle tracking experiments in Dynein mutants, supported by Table 1 and Figure 1E.

claim: The Dhc8-1 allele produces a functional motor protein that still moves, but significantly more slowly than the wild-type protein.
source: Thus, this allele produces a functional motor protein that still moves, but significantly more slowly than the wild-type protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the mutant still shows movement, but at reduced speed.

claim: The majority of bcd mRNA particles are transported by Dynein.
source: The strong reduction in the speed of bcd mRNA particles in Dhc8-1 homozygotes indicates that the majority are transported by Dynein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the strong reduction in speed in Dynein mutants.

claim: The Dhc8-1 mutant significantly reduces the amount of bcd mRNA localised to the anterior.
source: The Dhc8-1 mutant also significantly reduces the amount of bcd mRNA localised to the anterior (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from imaging of Dynein mutants, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The mobile fraction of bcd mRNA particles is unaffected in Dhc6-10/Dhc8-1 mutants (26% in wild-type versus 22% in mutant).
source: This does not seem to be due to reduced frequency of movement because the mobile fraction of bcd mRNA particles is unaffected in Dhc6-10/Dhc8-1 mutants (26% in wild-type versus 22% in mutant; Table 2, Table 2—source data 1, Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a primary finding from analysis of mobile fractions, supported by Table 2 and Figure 1G.

claim: Slower Dynein-dependent transport impairs the delivery of bcd mRNA to the oocyte anterior.
source: Thus, slower Dynein-dependent transport, presumably both from the nurse cells into the oocyte and within the oocyte, impairs the delivery of bcd mRNA to the oocyte anterior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Dynein mutants reduce both speed and anterior localization.

claim: Null mutations in the Kinesin heavy chain (Khc) disrupt the localisation of bcd mRNA, with the majority of oocytes showing spreading of the RNA along the anterior and lateral cortex.
source: Null mutations in the Kinesin heavy chain (Khc) also disrupt the localisation of bcd mRNA, with the majority of oocytes showing spreading of the RNA along the anterior and lateral cortex (Januschke et al., 2002) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature and confirmed by Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Kinesin-I transports Dynein to the oocyte posterior.
source: Kinesin-I transports Dynein to the oocyte posterior, indicating that the two motors can associate in the same complex, and Kinesin-I could therefore affect bcd mRNA indirectly, for example by recycling Dynein to the oocyte posterior for further rounds of minus end-directed transport, or by modulating the activity of Dynein (Januschke et al., 2002; Palacios and St Johnston, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Kinesin-I and Dynein can associate in the same complex.

evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Kinesin-I transports Dynein.

claim: The mobile fraction of bcd mRNA particles is nearly twice the proportion observed for osk mRNA.

evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data from this manuscript with data from previous literature.

claim: In Khc27 mutants, the mobile fraction of bcd mRNA particles more than doubled to 47%.

evidence: This is a primary finding from analysis of mobile fractions in Kinesin mutants, supported by Table 2 and Figure 1G.

claim: It is highly unlikely that Kinesin-I is responsible for a significant proportion of bcd mRNA particle movements.
source: Thus, both the speed and frequency of bcd mRNA particle motility are increased in the absence of Kinesin-I, making it highly unlikely that this motor is responsible for a significant proportion of the movements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that loss of Kinesin-I increases both speed and frequency of movements.

claim: bcd mRNA particles showed virtually no reversals of movement in either wild-type or Khc27 mutants (1.9% versus 1.5%, respectively).
source: Furthermore, bcd mRNA particles showed virtually no reversals of movement in either wild-type or Khc27 mutants (1.9% versus 1.5%, respectively), suggesting the RNA does not alternate between transport by motors of opposing polarity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from particle tracking experiments.

claim: bcd RNA does not alternate between transport by motors of opposing polarity.
source: Furthermore, bcd mRNA particles showed virtually no reversals of movement in either wild-type or Khc27 mutants (1.9% versus 1.5%, respectively), suggesting the RNA does not alternate between transport by motors of opposing polarity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low frequency of directional reversals.

source: Kinesin-I must therefore act by some other mechanism to reduce the speed of movement by another motor, presumably Dynein, for example by engaging in a tug of war.

claim: The slow allele, Khc23, has little effect on the fraction of mobile particles (25%), compared to 47% in the null allele.
